items.s: On a hot summer day in Paris, Erwan Leo ____ a new shop.

tfn.s: The Paris shop sells roughly fifty kinds of butter.
tfn.why: The text says: "It sells around fifty different types, including special salted varieties."

tfn.s: It was very hot in Paris when the shop opened.
tfn.why: The text says: "With temperatures close to 41°C, he worried that the fridges might struggle and customers might stay away."

tfn.s: The text says that butter is now a health food.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: "The new excitement does not mean butter has become a health food."

tfn.s: The shop plans to open branches in other countries.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text does not say whether the shop will open more branches.

tfn.s: Butter has always been loved as much as it is today.
tfn.why: The text says: "Butter was not always treated with this much love."

focus.note: Linking words join ideas. Ask yourself: is the second idea a result, a reason, a contrast or something at the same time?

tfn.s: A newspaper report in October 2026 described the butter trend.
tfn.why: The text says: "According to a Guardian report in October 2026, butter is appearing at fashionable events, on restaurant tables and across social media in increasingly elaborate forms."

tfn.s: Butter's nutritional concerns have gone away.
tfn.why: The text says the opposite: "There is also a tension between describing butter as a natural, comforting ingredient and pretending that the nutritional concerns have vanished."

tfn.s: Butter sales in France rose by a fifth in 2026.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text gives no figures for butter sales.

tfn.s: Some chefs think the butter displays are mainly about getting attention.
tfn.why: The text says: "Some chefs question whether extravagant butter displays are more about getting attention than enjoying food."

tfn.s: The report proves that people buy luxury butter because money is tight.
tfn.why: The text calls this "interpretation rather than something the report proves".

focus.note: Check what comes next. Words like despite need a noun, words like whereas need a full clause, and some join two sentences.

tfn.s: The writer suggests that butter's return owes more to food culture than to any change in nutritional guidance.
tfn.why: The text says the enthusiasm "does not erase those concerns" but highlights "the difference between nutritional guidance and food culture".

tfn.s: Most of the customers at Le Butter are tourists.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text mentions tourists stocking up but gives no breakdown of customers.

tfn.s: The writer treats packaging as irrelevant to the appeal of small luxuries.
tfn.why: The text says social media helps small pleasures catch on "when producers package them with the visual care" of jewellery or cosmetics.

tfn.s: Butter's unhealthy reputation in recent decades came from nutritional concerns, not from chefs disliking it.
tfn.why: The text says saturated fat gave butter an unhealthy reputation, while "Chefs have long valued butter".

tfn.s: Butter sales in Paris have doubled since the shop opened.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text gives no sales figures.

focus.note: At this level, notice register and grammar. Notwithstanding takes a noun, albeit takes an adjective or phrase, and hence follows a semicolon.

speak.title: Role-play: a trip to the butter shop
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: You've seen a shop that sells fifty kinds of butter. You want to spend Saturday morning there. Persuade your friend to come. Say why it's worth a trip.

b.text: You think queuing for butter is silly. You'd rather save money and cook at home. Ask questions, then agree on a plan you both like.

phrases: I'd love to go on Saturday.
Is it really worth queuing for?
I'd rather save my money, to be honest.
We could go early, so there won't be a queue.
Let's meet in the middle: shop first, then lunch at home.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: where did you decide to go, and who gave way?
